utterances.speaker: MR. LONDROVIC
utterances.text: Witness A, tell me, did you see any wounded people in the hospital?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONDROVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what nationality they were?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: What nationality?

utterances.speaker: MR. LONDROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: Do you think that I had the occasion to ask the wounded what their names were, whether they were Serbs, Croats, or Muslims? They certainly weren't Muslims or Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONDROVIC
utterances.text: If they were not Muslims or Croats, can we deduce from that that they were Serbs?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONDROVIC
utterances.text: Can we also say that by then the armed conflict had started between the Serbs, Muslims, and Croats?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONDROVIC
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Thank you, sir. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Thank you, Mr. Londrovic. Mr. Tochilovsky, do you wish to use your right to re-examine briefly? What do you want to do?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: Your Honours, the Prosecution doesn't have any further questions for the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Thank you, Witness A. I am now going to ask my colleagues, the Judges of the Trial Chamber, to clarify a few points, not at all to ask you to relive the Calvary you went through but just for the Judges to have a correct impression of what happened. I turn first to my colleague, Judge Riad.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Good afternoon, Witness A. I am going to call you "Witness A" because we mustn't call you otherwise, but that has nothing to do with our respect for your identity. Can you hear me well?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: Good afternoon. Yes, I hear you well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: (Interpretation) I should like to follow the painful path that you went through. You come from the village of Brcko, don't you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: From the town of Brcko.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: (Interpretation) The town of Brcko. I see. Until you left Brcko, you saw atrocities in the town, or did these occur after you left?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: I beg your pardon. I'm not quite sure I understood you well, but I shall try and answer it. I was in Brcko from the beginning of the conflict. The conflict started on May the 1st. In the part of the town called Grcica, and it is from that direction that firing could be heard. I lived at the other end or the opposite end of the town. All my neighbours and friends sought shelter in safe places. They were afraid because nothing good could come of the fire. We had been listening to the news and we knew what was happening in Sarajevo, in Croatia, so that we more or less knew what was taking place. And the conflict in the part of the town where I lived did not start until the 3rd of May, 1992, in the afternoon. As my house was close to the hospital, I went to the hospital. My mother was very ill, a serious patient. Because I hadn't been home for a couple of days, I went to hospital to see whether she had gone there to seek medical attention, as when I came home, I didn't find anyone there. When I arrived at the hospital, only a couple of hours after my arrival, the Chetniks barged into the hospital. Heading the four I had mentioned, and there were ten of them in all, I already mentioned Dusan Tadic; Pero, a former karate athlete; Zeljko, the taxi driver; Dragan Tanackovic; and the other four who had come from Serbia and whom I didn't know, whom I saw for the first time in my life.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: (Interpretation) If I may interrupt you? You said that they came from the territory of Serbia. How did you know that they came from Serbia? They were therefore not from Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: Well, you see, they were not from Bosnia, and I concluded this from the way they spoke because they speak the Ekavski dialect, whereas we in Bosnia, including the Serbs in Bosnia, we use the Ijekavski dialect, even though they're now trying to adjust to the Ekavski dialect, but this is common knowledge, and it is very easy to recognise the dialect and the accent, so there was no doubt in our minds where they came from.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Were they in uniform, Serbian uniforms, or were they civilians?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: No, they wore military camouflage uniforms with various caps. One of them had a hat. Others had red berets, two or three of them. One of them had a helmet on his head.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: (Interpretation) This camouflage uniform, is that combat gear? Is it combat gear?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: I think there's no difference. I know they were wearing camouflage uniforms under full combat gear, fully armed, armed to the teeth, and also I can't recollect exactly on which side of the shoulders, on the epaulets, they had ribbons which they changed. Every day they wore a different colour. I suppose this was to help them identify themselves.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Let me go on to another matter. You entered the Luka camp on the 11th of May, 1992. How and why were you arrested? Was there any particular reason? What were the grounds for the arrests that they were making of you and others? Was it random or was it a selection of people?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: You see, in the hospital, there were the nurses who were necessary to care for the patients and future wounded, and since the group that I belonged to was not necessary there -- we didn't have any medical training, and we were Muslims, with two exceptions.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: (redacted). The other exception was -- I'm sorry for mentioning the name. I will not mention the name of the other one. He was half Serb, half Croat. I think his mother was Serb and his father was Croat. All the others were Muslims.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: (Interpretation) You said you were arrested because you were Muslims. Was that the only reason? Was that a sufficient reason to be arrested?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: (Interpretation) When you were in the camp, you said that they made 100 people come out in groups of four every night, and only one or two would reappear, the others disappeared. On what basis were the people selected to go out, in your view, in order to be massacred? How were they selected? Was it absolutely at random, to get rid of everyone, or was some kind of reason given to determine the priority for the extermination of people?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: Let me repeat once again that when we arrived at Luka, no one took down our names, know whether we were rich or not, know what kind of education we had, who we were, what we were. They simply knew that we were Muslims and Croats, and the selection of victims was, I think, completely at random. They simply wanted to destroy us, to eradicate us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: (Interpretation) You also said, and I took note of it, that Jelisic said that there was no room here for the balijas. Did that mean that the balijas needed to be totally massacred or, perhaps, that they should simply leave the area? How did you understand that statement, that there was no room for balijas? Should they disappear from the planet or should they simply leave the area of Bosnia and go and live elsewhere?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: Judging by what was happening in Luka, in my opinion, as many Muslims as possible needed to be killed and, if possible, for them to be eradicated. But, by chance, people of other ethnic groups, Serbs -- I can't call them all Chetniks. They are not all the same because they were among the people who helped us. I don't want to mention any names because that could embarrass them, even though the war is long since over, not such a long time ago, actually. And the people who managed to leave with the help of those friends somehow managed to cross over to the free territory and to report what was happening. There were even Serbs who took photographs, at least these are things that I heard later, so that the International Community learned about what was happening, probably. And then it was thanks to the intervention of the International Community that this order had to be issued to stop the killing and mistreatment of people, and this was sometime around the 16th of May, as I have just mentioned. Their aim was to kill as many as possible, and those who were not killed, to have them resettled in other countries in Europe, or the world, or in other parts of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: (Interpretation) You just said that there were people who took photographs. There is, here, a rather strange photograph and a tragic one. It is Exhibit number 3. Who could have taken such a photograph of the execution of a man with the corpses on the ground? Were they Serbs taking these photographs? Who were they? It is a document tendered by the Prosecution, number 3. How could anyone go in and see this and take a photograph? The people who were executing people, did they act like the Nazis and take photographs of their misdeeds?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: To be quite honest, there may be two assumptions that could explain this photograph. They, themselves, may have taken it or, rather, they must have taken it, it must have been taken by a Serb, but a Serb who wanted to sell this somewhere abroad or to the media, maybe foreign media, or a Serb or a Chetnik who wanted to have a memento of how these two peoples were being destroyed, so that the third, their people, could continue to live. Because it is impossible that any Muslim could have got inside, especially into the Luka camp, because they couldn't even walk freely in town, despite the passes that were issued by the police. These passes were just a false hope for those who received them. They would get them today, they'd go home, and then the next day, they would be brought back. Either, as we already heard from the stories of others who were brought then, they would be released in the morning and killed in the evening in their own homes, or in the apartments, or flats where they had sought shelter because some of them couldn't go back to their own apartments. Others lived in parts of the town where fighting was still ongoing, so that it was unsafe there, and it was impossible to restore normality to life. So that my conclusion is that this photograph could not have been taken by a Muslim or a Croat.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: (Interpretation) You said that the accused, Mr. Jelisic, entered into the hangar and said, on the 16th of May, that an order had been issued to stop the killings, and everybody was happy. Did he also tell you, when he was doing the killings, that he had an order to do them or was it he, himself, who wanted to appear to be the big boss who had the right to decide about life and death?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: As I mentioned in my statement, which I gave on the 21st of May this year, he entered -- this is described very briefly in the statement, as are all the other incidents -- he entered, together with Major Djurkovic and another captain in uniform. I think he was a captain by rank. He was wearing a uniform of the former JNA, and he was accompanied by a couple of guards. And he simply said --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Just a moment, please. The uniform was the JNA uniform? He was a captain of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: Yes, of the former JNA. Major Djurkovic and this captain were wearing those uniforms.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Please continue.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: They entered, escorted by a couple of soldiers, guards, and we were told that he had received an order from the command - he knows best who from - that the order had come to stop the killing, the abuse, the mistreatment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: (Interpretation) I understand that very well. You told us that, but that was to stop the killing. But when executions were taking place, did they say that they were doing them under superior orders or was it as stated in the Prosecution brief, that Jelisic had absolute power to do what he wanted with the prisoners? Can you confirm that he had this absolute power, the accused, or was he executing orders, like at the end when he received orders to stop the executions?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: I didn't hear anyone give him any orders to kill, nor did he say that he had been given orders to kill. He simply did it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: (Interpretation) So he didn't say that he had orders, but he did tell you that he received orders to stop?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: That is the only occasion when he said that he had received orders to stop the killing and the mistreatment. That was the only occasion, during the time I was in the camp, that he told us that he had received any orders.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: (Interpretation) And after he stated that, did they, indeed, stop with the executions?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: He, alone, can know. After that, on rare occasions did someone else come to the camp. We would hear shots from the hangar. There were even some moans and pleas, but we didn't see that, but the mistreatment continued. Even he personally enjoyed mistreating and beating up two prisoners, whose names I will not mention now and, according to what one of them told us, he called up the Croatian military authorities to arrange an exchange for that particular man, one of the two, and for another prisoner who was also a Croat by nationality. And according to what this prisoner, who was beaten up, told us and whom I couldn't recognise, he was so badly beaten and disfigured from the beating, he told me that the accused had forced him to talk to someone from the military authorities in Croatia and to beg them to have him exchanged. And while he was talking to this person, a representative of the Croatian military authorities, by phone, Jelisic beat him with whatever he could get a hold of, even with the metal part of the fire hose, with spades, chairs, the police truncheon, simply with anything he could lay his hands on. As, according to what we were told by this prisoner, they refused any negotiation on a possible exchange, he continued to mistreat him and to beat him, and only when he lost consciousness did they bring him to the hangar door and left him there at the door. They called two prisoners to come and take him to his place because every time that man was taken out, and it was every night, after this mistreatment, he couldn't walk. The same happened with another prisoner, and it was terrible to look at these people. In my opinion, a human being is incapable of doing such a thing. Only a beast, an animal, can do it that has no heart, no feelings, a beast who simply kills without being hungry, who is killing out of pleasure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Are you talking about Jelisic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LONDROVIC
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Your Honours, I do apologise --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: I apologise for having to say this, but that is what I consider him to be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Just a moment, please. Mr. Londrovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LONDROVIC
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Your Honour, I, personally, and my colleagues have every understanding for the gentlemen, but because he said that he was a civilised person, I don't think he should insult the accused because the principle here is that one is innocent until proven guilty. So I should appeal to him not to call him a beast and insult him in that way.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: I said that I apologised to Their Honours and to the gentlemen from the Prosecution, to the Court officials, but sometimes I simply can't control myself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Mr. Londrovic, I think there is a question of dignity. The witness has taken a great deal of risk to come and testify here. I think that he experienced things which, fortunately for you and for me, at any rate, we have not experienced, and I don't know anyone who did, and perhaps one should understand that a certain number of expressions may escape him, and this is the first time that he is in the presence of the accused, in the same room as he, so perhaps I think we should try and understand. Judge Riad, you may continue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: (Interpretation) I heard you explain how those atrocities were committed, but my question was, and perhaps you don't need to use these expressions like "beast" and all that, but did he have pleasure, did he gain pleasure from doing this? Because one can kill following orders, one can kill and execute, and one can really enjoy executing somebody, and that is what I'd like to hear you answer, rather than using expressions such as "beast" and so on, because beasts kill only to eat.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: What I have stated, if you will recall it from my statement, is that precisely at the time when I was in that group which was called out when the accused was there, when he killed a victim, and he said, "One balija less," I don't think that this was killing on orders. I think that this was killing out of pleasure, out of some kind of hate against my people. This victim could have been a Croat, could have been a Muslim, could have been a Catholic. It was simply out of hate, out of pleasure, out of desire to annihilate one or the other people, to destroy a people both psychologically and physically. My opinion is that those of us who survived from this group, we all believed that what they were trying to do was to inflict as much pain upon us as possible so that we could see our friends, our neighbours dead there, and that we would pass this on to those who had stayed in the hangar so that they would be psychologically destroyed, so that they would destroy their self-respect, that they would humiliate them, so that they would beg for their lives even more. In other camps where I stayed afterwards, we were offered to change our names, to change our faith, not to be Muslim anymore, to be a Serb, to be Orthodox. Just as I was offered it, other members of my people and of the Croats were offered the same. They simply wanted to destroy us, both mentally and physically.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Please take some rest. Please try to relax and take some rest.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: I want to continue because I believe it is going to -- I will feel even worse later on. I can go on, but I don't want to talk about this anymore. If you have any additional questions, Your Honours, please, do ask them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: (Interpretation) All right. I don't know if you said this or if the Prosecutor said this in his preliminary statement, but I remember hearing that Jelisic was saying that he was proud of the fact that he could kill 20 or so Muslims before even taking his morning coffee. Did you say that or did the Prosecutor say that? At any rate, did you hear Jelisic say that at some point in the camp?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: I did not hear it from him directly, but I heard it from others who were with me in the camp.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: (Interpretation) And my last question to you will be this one: I think that you yourself told us that Jelisic had stated that all Muslims were guilty, but guilty of what? Did he specify what Muslims were guilty of?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: He did not explain why we were guilty, simply the Muslims were guilty, all Muslims were guilty. That was -- how shall I think of it? -- because we are Muslims, they called us a Turkish gang. Why? I was born in Bosnia. I was a Muslim from Bosnia, not from Turkey. They called us balijas. This is a word that comes from times past. I don't even know when. Maybe my grandfathers, great-grandfathers would know that word and its original meaning. From what I know, at that time it meant a rich peasant, but they called us balijas, as a peasant, I guess. If you wanted to offend somebody in the territory of the former Yugoslavia, if he lived in the city, if he was a city-dweller, he would be called a peasant, "You ugly peasant," and that would be an offence; and this word "balija" could be interpreted and is interpreted as an offence. I myself do consider it an offensive word, as well as if somebody calls me a Turkish gangster and if they curse my mother and things like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Thank you, Witness A, for answering my questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Thank you, Judge Riad. Judge Rodrigues, do you have any questions you would like to put to the witness?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Yes, thank you, Mr. President. One question only.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My apologies, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Please take your time, Witness A. Would you like to take a break? Would you like to take some rest? Would you like a five-minute break?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no. Please, go on. I can go on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Witness A, I have only one question that I would like to put to you. Yesterday, you stated that in the Luka camp, you had heard some songs saying, among other things, that the balijas would be exterminated. Do you remember telling us about these songs yesterday?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour. Perhaps there may have been a slight misinterpretation. Yesterday I said that songs could be heard and shouting could be heard, Chetniks shouting, "Balijas, we'll eradicate you, we'll destroy you." And the songs which were played on the cassette player were songs about some Chetnik warlords from World War II and they were celebrating those warlords through those songs. What they did in battles, they exulted them in these songs. Even we had to sing those Chetnik songs. We were ordered to do so. If it was noticed that somebody was not singing along, he would be beaten; if somebody was not singing loud enough, he would fare the same.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: (Interpretation) But let's go back to my question, my initial question. These songs you heard in the camp, who sang them and why were they sung, and, in fact, was it a cassette which was played, or were individuals actually singing these songs? Where did they actually come from: from individuals or from tapes that were played in the camp?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: These songs were played from cassettes which had been recorded even before the war. They had them. I could hear them in town. They would try to sing along; in other words, to sing along with the voice that was on that tape. They would sing about Draza Mihajlovic, of a certain person called Sindjelic, and other Chetnik cut-throats from World War II. In between the songs, they were shouting how we all should be annihilated, we should be eradicated, and then they also played a Bosnian song. If I recall correctly, it was sung by a Bosnian Muslim, and I'm just going to give you the title of the song which was about how Bosnia is crying, which described the suffering of people throughout Bosnia, because this song was recorded in my town just as the war was beginning in Zvornik, the war was already in Bijeljina, in Sarajevo, and other parts of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and while playing this song, they looked to see whether any one of us would try to sing it. It was a mournful song; it was very sad for us because we saw what was going on around us. Before the war, in our town, we were not aware what was going on in Bijeljina, Zvornik, Sarajevo, and other areas of Bosnia. Only when we experienced, when we saw with our own eyes what was going on, then we realised what had happened to other people, and we became very attached to this song. It became very meaningful to us. But woe to us if anybody would try to sing this song. They would beat these people up. This was really to kill us within, to kill us inside, and it wasn't just once that they did this, they did it at least ten times.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Thank you, Witness A. I don't have any further questions for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Thank you, Judge Rodrigues. As for myself, I have only a few questions I would like to put to you, Witness A. I know that you are very tired. Let's go back to what happened before you were arrested. Just before your arrest, did you take part in any military action? Were you in any way involved with the military formations on the ground? Were you engaged politically? Did you play some kind of particular role militarily or politically before your arrest?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. I was a soldier of the former army before the war, and I completed those duties. I completed them in 1981. Had I known what would happen, I would never have done it. Before the war, I was a member of the then Communist party, but the last three or four years before the war, I was a member of no party. I was not interested in the party. I had my own family. I was preoccupied with other things. I was not interested in politics.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Now I would like to ask you some questions about life inside the camp. Were any activities organised on a regular basis? For example, were you all reassembled in the morning? Was there a roll call? Were you obliged to hear some politically-motivated speeches, or did you just remain in the hangar without doing anything special? Were you left to yourselves in the hangar? Was there a roll call in the morning? Were you called out? I haven't quite understood all what you said about life inside the camp.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: During the period of killings until the order was issued to stop the killing and mistreatment, there were no lists, just as I said. There were no activities except the sad one when we had to, both myself and the other ones who survived, to load our dead compatriots onto the trucks, and as I said, some were not loaded onto the trucks, some were just thrown into the Sava River, some were piled up and then transported somewhere else. There were no other activities except for the activities of having to listen to their insults, their tortures, their beatings, because they would enter and we would sit on the concrete. They would just enter, and they called us, just as I said, Turkish gang and so on and so forth, cursed our mothers. I don't want to repeat myself anymore.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Of course not. I don't want you to repeat anything you've said before. When three or four detainees were called outside the hangar and taken outside the hangar, apart from those who did come back alive and healthy, in a sense, were there any detainees who came back hurt? I'm sorry. My question is the following: Among the four, three or four detainees who were taken outside the hangar, all those who were beaten outside the hangar were killed afterwards, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: Let me give you an example. The group with which I came out, all four of us were beaten and insulted, and all the victims were beaten until they were forced to lie down on the pavement and put their head against the grate and then the perpetrator would step on their back and shoot in the back of the head. The rest of us would also be hit while we were carrying the victim or while we waited around, waiting for the selection of the next victim, or we would re-enter the hangar. But as far as the wounding of any of us who survived by firearm, no, nobody was injured or wounded in that way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) The impression we get is that the accused was managing everything but there was no real commander in the camp; nobody was controlling all that was done inside the camp. But this camp, did anybody know about it? Did the ICRC, for example, know about this camp, or was it a camp that was situated outside the town and that nobody knew about?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: What shall I say to that? I don't believe -- it is possible, as I answered one of the questions before, I believe it was a question posed by one of Your Honours, one of your colleagues, I believe that it is possible that some of the pictures, like this one here (indicating), have gone out to the world, and it is possible that one of them did take a picture which was then published, and so they may have felt that they were under pressure by the International Community and so they felt that they had to transfer us, to stop with killings and torture; it is possible that this is why we were transferred to the Batkovic camp, in order that we would not be found by the humanitarian organisations in Luka, even though we were not allowed to talk in Batkovic either. I was, for instance, not found by the International Red Cross there; I was only found in Doboj in 1993 by the international organisations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Thank you very much, Witness A. We have no further questions for you, but there is one thing I would like to say: If you feel you want to add anything to what you have already told us, if there is anything you would like to say publicly in front of this Tribunal, please do so now. As far as we are concerned, we have no other questions for you, but feel free to express anything you would like to add.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know. Maybe -- maybe I can ask a question of sorts, if I can ask your permission for that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Of course, you may put your question. Of course. If it's a question to the Judges, just put the question to us and we'll try to answer to the best of our ability.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Since the accused, as I can see, has not one Defence counsel, but I realise that out of three counsel, two come from the occupied territories of Bosnia and Herzegovina, I would like to ask them, because it is impossible that the Tribunal should be paying for three counsel, I would like to ask the Defence, in fact, the two counsel from the occupied Bosnia and Herzegovina, whether they ever thought with whose money the accused is paying them, and is it possible that my 5.500 German marks is among that money and the money of the other persons who were robbed by them?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Witness A, I'm sorry, but you cannot put this question to Defence counsel. Of course, by coming here, you have greatly contributed to our work and you, as all of us, wish for a better world and a civilised world. The only way for us to answer to barbaric behaviour is to resort to civilised means and to behave ourselves in a civilised way. The accused has a right to have a fair trial. If he is considered to be guilty, we will say so on the last day of this trial. Let us not speak about money. Let us not put this kind of issue to Defence counsel. I am sure that all the people who are working for this trial share and greatly sympathise with you and with all that you have been through, but we are not an investigating committee, we are Judges. Our aim is to try the facts, to see what the accused may have done, to see what he hasn't done. It is not an easy task, but all the people that are working and that you see in this courtroom are trying to help us achieve this aim, and I'm taking this opportunity to thank everybody, because we are all trying to achieve a very difficult aim. We are all faced with huge responsibilities. Maybe I am disappointing you. Maybe this answer is a disappointment to you, but I cannot allow this debate to be entered into in this courtroom. If you don't have anything further to add, I will only just say that we all thank you for coming here. We are well aware of what it has meant for you to come before this Tribunal. You are still young, and we wish you a more serene and happy life from now on. You have been granted a number of protective measures. We need to raise the curtains to allow the witness to leave the courtroom, so maybe we can take a break. And if the next witness is a protected witness, then he can be brought in the courtroom before we resume the hearing. We will resume our work at 16.00 hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: (The witness entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) The hearing is resumed. Please have the accused brought in. (The accused entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Witness B, can you hear me? It is the President of the Trial Chamber who is addressing you. Will you remain standing for a few minutes? Will you first identify the name written on a piece of paper as yours without repeating it? Do you have the name? The Prosecutor is giving it to the usher, and please check that that is, indeed, your name.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) You will remain standing for a few minutes to read your solemn declaration given to you by the usher. Please proceed. Read it, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Thank you, Witness B. You may be seated. You are a witness enjoying protective measures. Let me explain. At the request of the Prosecution, the Chamber has granted these measures which means that the hearing is public. You may speak without fear because these measures are such that you cannot be recognised or identified. Nevertheless, I call on the parties to be very careful that your name or the name of another person may not slip out. We thank you for coming. First, the Prosecution will be asking you questions in these proceedings against the accused, Goran Jelisic, who is here present. After that, you will be answering questions by the attorneys of Jelisic and then by the Judges. Mr. Prosecutor, the floor is yours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Witness B. Witness B, let me ask you some background information first. How old are you?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. We can't hear the witness very well. Could he speak into the microphone?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: I will just repeat my question. Can you tell us, how old are you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Fifty-three.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: Are you of Muslim ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: Where did you live before the war?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: In Brcko, the part of the town called Grcica.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: Witness B, can you tell us whether you were detained in Luka camp? Were you detained there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: I was. Can I begin with the date?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Speak simply, in your own words without any fear. You are addressing Judges, expressing yourself as you wish. If you forget something, don't worry. The Prosecutor will either interrupt you or he will come back to questions which he considers useful to put to you, so please proceed.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: I was at home until May the 6th when soldiers came and took us to Laser. I was in Laser for two days, from the 6th until the 8th. On the 8th, we went by bus from Laser to Luka. About half past one or 2.00 in the afternoon, I saw --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Excuse me. What month was this and what year?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: It was the 8th of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: May I interrupt you, Witness B?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: Did you see Goran Jelisic upon your arrival at Luka?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: I assume that Goran Jelisic was in Laser on the 6th of May because I recognised him on the 8th of May when I got to Luka. I recognised him by his speech. On the 6th of May, he was there. He came in the evening with somebody known as Cupa and with another guard.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: Could you make it more clear? Was it in Laser Company?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: Please continue.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: In the restaurant.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: Is that the place where you first saw Goran Jelisic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: I saw him for the first time. It was dark, and there was no light in the restaurant. But anyway, when I arrived on the 8th of May, I recognised his voice. I didn't know that it was Goran Jelisic, but I recognised his voice on the 8th of May when I saw him.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: Did Goran Jelisic introduce himself, either in Laser Company or in Luka camp or in both?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: He didn't introduce himself in the Laser Company. They entered there. They started shouting. They started beating, seizing money and personal documents. A couple of times, they leaned people against the wall, and this Cupa would hit them. They would curse at each other saying, "Don't hit him so hard. Let me beat him a little." I was scared. This was the first time I had seen people being beaten and money being stolen from them. Then he said to the guard, "Cock your rifle and point it at them," meaning us, and that is what the guard did.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: Excuse me. Who said that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: I think it was Goran Jelisic. It was his voice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) When you answer, will you please face the Judges? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: Do you remember Goran Jelisic introducing himself?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: In the Laser, he didn't introduce himself. In Luka, he did. When we got off the bus, we all entered the hangar. And as the bus approached the hangar, the door was open, and I could see that the hangar was full of people. The bus stopped right in front of the door. There were guards there, there were a lot of them, and they told us to get off and to go inside. As we entered, on the right-hand side, there was a big box, into which personal documents were thrown, ID cards, driving licenses, passports, if anyone had one, and they ordered me too, as I came off the bus, to throw my documents there. I had my ID card, and I put it into the box which was overflowing with these documents, and then we entered. When all of us from the bus had got in, I was in the second bus, I saw that it was full of people. The left-hand side of the hangar was full of people. One young woman was sitting on a chair to the right, the guards were on the sides at the entrance to the hangar, and she was sitting on this chair, and I saw that she had some kind of band-aid on her chest, and she said that the Muslims had cut off her breast. She was an attractive young woman, and I saw that she had this breast, and she said that the breast had been cut off. So when we came off the bus, Goran entered, and he saw how many of us there were. And he laughed and said that there were many of us, and he started to say, how come we had stayed in Brcko. He said that we had started the war, that we wanted the war against the Serbs, and no one had any such ideas. We wanted the war, according to him, not they, that we hate them. Then he ordered the guards -- he introduced himself. He said, "My name is Goran Jelisic, known as Adolf. You will get to know me well. I am the boss here." And we stood there listening to him. We had to. And he behaved boastfully and then arrogantly. And then he told the guards, "Collect all those documents," and they did, and they took them across the way to the office. Goran followed them. He didn't come back, neither Goran nor the other two who had carried the documents. The rest stayed to watch over us. You know what the position of prisoners is.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: Witness B, may I interrupt you. So Goran Jelisic, you made it clear that he introduced himself as Adolf. But my next question is: Did you see killings committed by Goran in Luka?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: Can you tell the Court about those killings?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Yes, I have to tell you things in order. This, that I was telling you about, lasted for about an hour and a half or two. Then Goran Jelisic came carrying these personal documents, and the guard followed him, also carrying some ID cards and passports. And then he said, "I'm going to start reading and whose name I call will be executed," and he said, "Whose name I call must go outside," and then he smiled and said, "Don't be afraid. I was joking. The names I read out, the people will go home." And quite a number of people went out that day, and, indeed, they got discharge papers and they left. When he came back a second time, he was carrying two documents. He read out the names of two men, "Zahirovic" was the surname, but they were not from Brcko. And he asked, "What are the two of you doing in Brcko?" And these two men said, they told the truth, "We came to visit our relatives to celebrate May Day with them." He said, "You haven't come to celebrate May Day. You have come upon orders. It's not for May Day that you have come. You have some kind of a plan." But they insisted that they came for May Day, but the war started. And then he took out these two men, and he said, "As you've come to celebrate May Day, this will be your last." He took them out and they were killed. He asked for three volunteers to carry one of them. Then he called for another three volunteers, and they carried the second. I don't know where they were taken. In any event, both of them were killed, and he said, "That will be your May Day celebration."

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: Can you describe other killings you saw in the camp committed by Goran Jelisic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Yes. On that day, he had killed two already. Then night came, the killings continued. He would always come asking for three or four volunteers. I hadn't been called out yet, but my turn would come. The younger and braver ones went out. In any event, the killings started, and whoever carried a body said that Goran was there with a pistol next to the grate where the people were killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: Can you tell the Court about the killings which were committed on the day when you cleaned Goran Jelisic's office?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Yes, I was cleaning. The guard came because all the younger men had to go and work elsewhere, and I was well advanced in age. I also applied to clean a hangar. It had to be cleaned well, and we did clean it. As I was coming out of the hangar, and I was going from the hangar I had cleaned to the one where we had been detained, the guard said to me, "Old man," or something, "can you clean this office too," and I said, "I can." So I entered the office. There was broken glass on the floor. They had eaten some roast lamb, and there were broken bottles. I cleaned it well. And I heard Goran's voice, and I got frightened immediately. I hurried up. I hurried to finish the cleaning so as to reach my hangar, and after a couple of minutes, I finished the cleaning. I put my jacket on a sign next to the grate, I think it was a traffic sign prohibiting parking, and I had left my jacket there because it was quite warm.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: May I interrupt you, Witness B.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: If I could have the assistance of the usher, Mr. President, in placing the Prosecutor's exhibit in front of the witness.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Yes, if you can, yes, the picture. It would be better so that I can show how it was.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Exhibit number 6, and the sheet of paper on which the name of the witness appeared was Exhibit number 5.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: Witness B, have you had an opportunity to indicate some locations on the photo relevant to your testimony?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: The image is not stable, but here it is. This is the grate. There should have been a traffic sign here, but it's gone. Here was the pavement. I cleaned behind here, this office there. Around here, where this pole is, was where I would come, and I was about here when Goran entered (indicating), entered the hangar, and there was a young man, dark-haired. I came to this side, to where my implements were, and he said, "What are you doing here?" And I sort of fell silent because I sort of lost my ability to speak, and so I just pointed that I was cleaning here, and then he said, "Stop where you are." This was here (indicating), almost at the grate itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: Witness B, are you referring to point X-4 as the place where you were staying?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Yes. This is where my jacket was, and he picked it up and he said, "Is this yours?" And he said, "Don't take it. Just stand here." So he took the young man from this hangar and took him to the grate, and the young man came over here (indicating). He said, "Kneel down," which he did. He said, "Put your head down." You can see the edge of the pavement here. But he said, "Place it right next to the grate." And Goran stepped up and he fired two shots in the back of the head. This was the first time that I saw a murder, a killing. The body just collapsed. And then he said, "Three volunteers." He had a strong voice. He said, "Three volunteers." And I saw that the volunteers were coming out. They picked up the dead body. Two of them picked it up by a shoulder each and a third by the legs, and they took it behind the shed, behind this structure here (indicating), and a guard escorted them as they went to throw it into a canal. Again, I reached to pick up my jacket, and he said, "Stop. Don't." And so I stood still. I still could not muster any voice. I was all in sweat. It was the first time that I had seen a murder. Then he came out with another young man; he was blond, had a broken nose. He did the same thing. He brought him here, he ordered him to kneel down, he knelt down, then he told him, "Put your forehead against the edge of the pavement." The young man refused to do it, and then he ordered him again to do it. They started going back and forth. He started cursing him. The young man still refused to put it there. Then he grabbed him by the neck and pushed it down, pushed the whole head down to the pavement and stepped on him, and then he pulled the trigger. The young man fell, and then again he called for three volunteers. Another three volunteers came out of the hangar, and they carried him behind the shed where the dead bodies were being thrown. I still stood there. When the second person was killed, he said -- he asked me, what did I do? I was still without any voice. I still couldn't produce a voice and I was all sweaty, and I just stood there. And then he said, "Well, are you done?" And I kind of signalled that I was. He went into the office to see, and it was really all spic and span, he even complimented me, and then he said, "This is really well done. You can take your jacket. You're not going to be killed." I did not know whose office this was, I just knew that I had to clean it. Then he told me, "Go back into the hangar. You're not going to be killed."

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: Did Goran Jelisic make comments about these killings? Did he ask you whether you could do that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Yes. He asked -- this was on 9 May. It had just dawned. Between 7.30 and 8.00, he brought in a man. He was a tall man, strong, he may have weighed 100, 120 kilos even. So he brought in this man in the hangar, and I saw that his hand was bloody. His right ear had been cut off, so he was carrying his ear in his hand, and I saw -- and he also was mopping his head with a handkerchief. We all got up - all of us were sitting around against the wall of the hangar - we all got up, and he said to this man, he said, "Crouch." He crouched in the middle of the hangar facing us. The blood was still dripping and he was still trying to clean the blood and he was still holding his ear in his hand, and I asked myself, Good God. Can something like this exist, that there is this sight of a man holding his own ear in his hand? He knew that we were predominantly Muslim. He said, "Muslim brothers and, if there are any Croats among us, please kill me so that this criminal does not kill me." And Goran went around offering the pistol to one after another in order to kill him, and then he said -- he said, "You are no people. You are nothing. You should all be killed." There was another guard with Goran. He had a sword or a sabre which was more than one metre long, and as Goran saw that none of us dared to do this -- and this man kept begging us to kill him. So Goran ordered, "Get up." And as this man was leaving, he ran towards him, and as he was -- he was about to leave, he hit him with this sabre, as this man who was still holding that ear in his hand, and this man sort of bent a little and came out, and as he was crossing over to this grate, he was killed. This was not even ten seconds later. Then Goran asked for four volunteers this time because he was a heavy man, so four men came out and threw him behind the shed where the rest of the bodies were thrown; and so this poor man with his ear cut off, that was his end.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: Witness B, let me ask you a question again about that incident at Goran Jelisic's office when you were standing at the traffic sign. After the killing of those people, did he express anything about his feeling about those killings?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: You know how he behaved? I think that he took pleasure in doing this because he was so powerful, he was viewed as a god. It was nothing for him to kill a man. He believed himself to be the most powerful person in the world, and he was, in Brcko. I cannot understand this. He was a young man, a handsome man, and to do this ... But he killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: Did Goran Jelisic ask you whether you can do the same?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: He did, yes, and he asked me this, and I couldn't talk. He was offering us to take the pistol. "He is your man," he said. "Kill him." How? How come? He didn't do anything to me. How come -- I can't kill a fly, let alone a man.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: Did he ask you such a question at his office where several people were killed at the grate? Did he ask you why you were so scared, and did he express anything about that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Yes. He said, "What kind of man are you? You do not dare kill anybody, beat anybody. Look at us." We all had to stay silent. There was nothing for me to say. What was I going to say? I cannot hate somebody, let alone kill him. And, I don't know, he may have taken pleasure in this. A young man, to be doing this, I cannot understand that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: Did he say that "it is nice to kill people"?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Yes, he did say that. He said that it was nice to kill. "You cannot kill." He said that we asked for a war. We never did. Who needs a war? And apparently we had started the war. This is what we were told. And it's well-known who started it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: Witness B, did Goran Jelisic mention the number of Muslims he had killed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: No, he did not mention that. He simply entered the hangar, he would stand there, and he would point out. He'd say, "You come out. You and you and you." And he, for the most part, sought out young men. And sometimes he had some kind of a piece of paper and he was looking for specific names. He would ask, "Is such and such a person here in the camp?" And we didn't know them, but -- we didn't know who these people were; he could have known that. But we didn't matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: Did he mention that there is a figure of those Muslims that he would like to reach in killing?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Yes, he mentioned when he came, whenever he came, he would be -- not very inebriated but sometimes he would come, and one time he said -- it was either 76 or 86, one of those two figures. I'm not sure of this, which number, which figure is the precise one; I heard him say that, but I don't remember well. He said either 76 or 86, one of those two. And he said, "I haven't reached --" I don't remember what number he mentioned, to what number he was going to go.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: Witness B, can you tell the Court what happened to Ribic Smail and who was Mr. Ribic Smail?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: I think that Smail Ribic was the number 2 man in the local municipal government in Brcko. I believe that he was like a deputy, but he was a prominent person. Can I tell about the incident?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Please go ahead, Witness B; that is, if Mr. Tochilovsky has no more precise question to ask you. But if you want to give us your explanation of this particular event, please do so, but please face the Judges when answering the questions.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Let me tell it. He took him in the car, that is, he took Smail and a Serb. I had not known that he was a Serb, but later I heard from a neighbour that he was a Serb, so he was a Serb; and apparently this Serb wanted to take Smail, to help Smail go to Germany to where his wife was, and they were both captured, and Goran took out the both of them. I immediately recognised Smail. Five or six days before, I saw him in this political meeting in Brcko, and I thought to myself: He's not going to come out of Luka alive. So he took them out of the car. They were holding hands, and he was going to show the people what love there was between Serbs and Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: Excuse me, Witness B. To whom are you referring to when you say "he"? Was that Goran Jelisic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Goran Jelisic, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: Please continue.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: So he said, "Look how they love each other, a Serb and a Muslim? We beat them so much in Bijeljina that we couldn't separate them. That's how much they love each other and that's how we brought them to Luka." And indeed, Smail came -- got out of the car first, and I saw them holding hands. They barely managed to enter the hangar. They entered the hangar and off to the right -- they went to the right. I saw that they were barely walking. And so they put them right there immediately. As they were walking, they just sort of collapsed, and Goran left. Then later, they came, that is, the guards came, and they beat them again. This neighbour of mine who was sitting next to me, who knew the Serb, told me, "This one is a Serb. And do you know who the other one is?" And I said, "Yes, I do." So the young man started shivering, and I said, "Just calm down. This is how things are right now." The Serb asked for water. He was thirsty. A large bucket of water was brought in, and this man brought them a bucket filled with water, and they were still lying down, they couldn't get up, and then he threw the water over the two of them. He said, "Here's the water." That bucket was filled with water. And then they started coming in, the guards, and Goran with them, and they beat them. He seemed to be particularly irritated by the fact that these two were fond of one another. And then that night, it was probably between 2.00 and 8.00, everybody came and beat them. They were all completely beat up. I was in another hangar; that is, it is the same hangar, but I was in another part. And if you show me the picture, I can point it out to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: What happened to those two men?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: It could have been 7.30 or 8.00 -- this is how we estimated, because it was dark, we didn't have watches -- first the Serb was killed and then the other one was killed, and the volunteers carried them out, and they also were then ordered to bring water from the bathroom to wash the blood. I was in another part of the hangar. As the door -- it was a large door but there was a little crack, so I saw there was a little canal and I saw blood running or -- so they had to wash it with buckets of water so that all the blood would be washed away. So, anyway, the two of them were both killed, and he said, "If I am capable of killing a Serb, what about you Muslims? You're not even a people. When I can kill my own fellow Serb, then you can all be killed."

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: Witness B, did you carry dead bodies in Luka?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: While carrying those bodies, did you see piles of bodies, and how many bodies were in the pile?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Yes, let me tell you. There were some people who carried quite a number of bodies, and after awhile, they were too afraid to continue doing that, so I decided at one point that I had to also volunteer. When they asked for a volunteer, I volunteered, together with another two men. And so we approached this grate. There was a dead body lying by it. I took the body by the legs, and the other two took it each by an arm, and we were told by a guard to take it behind a shed. And we may have crossed about 30 metres, and we saw that he was a pretty heavy man, that the body was heavy. When we came to this canal, I saw 10 to 15 bodies there. I was shivering as I was holding those legs, and then this guard said, "Guys, you have to swing him so that you can hoist him on top of the pile," and that's when I saw that there were at least 10 to 15 bodies there, because there was quite a pile there already.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: Do you know how the bodies were taken from the camp?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Yes, we could hear trucks in the night, but the people who carried the bodies out, they probably know exactly. They probably loaded them onto the truck and drove them off somewhere, I don't know where, but the trucks would come at night, the big Bimex trucks that used to transport meat.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: Witness B, did you see Goran Jelisic when you moved dead bodies?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: I did. I saw him. I carried four bodies. When I carried the first body, Goran was standing there with a pistol. He wasn't afraid of anyone. He was the boss. The second body that I carried, there was a smaller pile just behind the shed, and the third body that I carried, I carried it behind the hangar on the railroad. There were five or six men, and I saw that they were lying down and their heads were put across the rail tracks. The fourth body that I carried was also to the tracks, and I saw three or four men. One of them was in pyjamas. I think he used to be in the hospital. And as I carried this body, the body of the killed man, the guard told me to put his head on the track, and I said, "Why? Why should we do that?" And he said, "Well, don't you see? This is their pillow." And that is what we did. He was gurgling, the man hadn't died yet, but all their heads were on the tracks, and he said, "This is their pillow." There were four of us on that occasion. We put the body there. I was the fourth, the last one, the younger ones went in front to get to the hangar as soon as possible, and then the guard said to me, "So you're the last one," and I thought that I was going to get killed, but he told me, "Take a bucket and a broom and wash the area from the grate to the rail track so that there will be no traces." As I ran cleaning this area, I saw Goran next to the grate, and I had just finished. The guard was standing by me all the time. And he said, "Make sure you clean it well so that no traces of blood are left," and I had to do it, and I did. And then he said, "You've cleaned it well. Take the bucket back." Then I saw three volunteers carrying another killed man where I had already cleaned, and I said to the guard, "Look, I've just cleaned it and there's more blood again," and he said, "Just keep quiet and go back in. Someone else will clean this."

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: Witness B, how were you supposed to behave while carrying dead bodies for Goran Jelisic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: It is hard to describe it. I sometimes prayed to God that I'd be killed too because I couldn't watch it anymore, but you just had to do these things. You don't even feel fear. You just had to carry those bodies, and you had to do whatever they told you to do. I wasn't even afraid anymore. I could have laid down with those dead bodies. I didn't feel any fear. You just had to do this, and I thought to myself, "I can't hope to get out of this alive and go back to my family." I thought it was all over for us.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: Before I ask you the next question, I just want to remind you that you're not supposed to mention any names which would reveal your identity. My next question is: Do you know of any incidents where bodies were thrown into the Sava River?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: All these people who were carried in some sort of a sheet, they were thrown into the Sava. My neighbour, for instance, he carried bodies that were thrown into the Sava. All the people who were on the rail track behind the hangar were taken to the Sava and thrown in. The people who threw them in know. They were loading these bodies, and I don't know exactly what was happening, but I know that a number of them were thrown into the Sava. These were volunteers that had to do this in the evening.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: Did Goran Jelisic exercise authority over other camp staff and over detainees in Luka?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: He was the most powerful man there, and all the Serbs feared him. He was the greatest. Everyone was afraid of him. Even the soldiers were afraid of Goran because he was the boss.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: Can you tell the Court how the killings in the camp were stopped?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: One morning it had dawned, we were all awaiting what would happen next, and Goran entered with a captain. By the way he spoke, I guessed that he was a Montenegrin. And Goran was carrying a piece of paper because all of us had been interrogated for exchange and for labour around town, as if it appeared that they wouldn't be killed, but nobody believed it. And then he came with this paper, and he lined us up, and he said, "Let me read you the order." I think it was around the 18th of May. We didn't really know the date. We guessed. He started reading. Anyway, the world appeared to have learned about the killings in Luka in Brcko, and then he said, "Was anyone killed here?" And we didn't dare to say anything, we said "No," and the whole world had learned of the Luka in Brcko. And he was reading this, and he said, "As of today, you must know that not a single man will be killed with a bullet but from beatings. If anyone succumbs, that's another matter, but anyway, no one in Luka may be killed from now on." We were happy but we didn't believe it, and that is how it was from that day on. Not a single man was killed with a bullet from that day on.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: Witness B, you were detained in the Batkovic camp as well; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: Did you see Goran Jelisic in Batkovic? Did he visit the Batkovic camp?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Yes, he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: Can you describe that visit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: I think it was September because I was released on the 12th of October. There were two hangars too. There were more people in the first hangar, and they separated us into the second hangar, and we heard that Goran Jelisic had arrived. I was terrified because there were about ten of us from Luka in this hangar there. What he was looking for, I don't know. He came to this hangar, and the director said that there were some people from Brcko there, and we all laid down and covered ourselves with blankets. He entered the hangar and he asked the guard, "Tell me, is there anyone from Luka from the month of May," and he said, no, that they had all been exchanged. He didn't believe him and he said, "That can't be right. There must be at least one or two of them," and this one said, "No, all the people from Luka have been exchanged." He was irritated and angry, and he left. I don't know what he really wanted, but I nearly died of fear. What he was looking for, I don't know, but thank God this director said that there wasn't a single man from Luka, and there were at least ten of us there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness B.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: Mr. President, I have concluded the direct examination, and I would like to ask that the exhibit which was shown by the Prosecutor to the witness be admitted into evidence, if the Defence have no objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Are there no objections on the part of the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I think not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Very well. Who is going to cross-examine this witness? It can only be one of the Defence counsel. We have another quarter of an hour. Witness B, you're not too tired to recall all these painful experiences? Can you hold on for another quarter of an hour or so, and then we will adjourn until tomorrow? We are not meeting in the morning. I just take advantage to inform the Prosecutor and the Defence that we will be resuming work tomorrow at 2.00 p.m. If you feel well enough, Mr. Londrovic, you are going to cross-examine. You are now going to be asked questions by the attorneys for the Defence. Mr. Londrovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LONDROVIC
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Your Honours, if I may suggest that we adjourn so that we can have more time to prepare for the cross-examination. You were kind enough today to allow both of us to cross-examine today, that is, Mr. Greaves and myself, and we would take advantage of the time this evening and tonight to prepare ourselves well for the cross-examination tomorrow, and it will be only one of us, so we don't want to disrupt the rules in any sense any further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Is there any objection on the part of the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: The Prosecution has no objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Since the Prosecution agrees, this will allow the witness to recover a little. In any event, we have no hearing in the morning because one of the Judges is busy with another case, and we can prepare for a rather long afternoon tomorrow. Mr. Registrar, we will begin at 2.00 p.m. Then you can prepare for the cross-examination. The hearing is adjourned. The registrar has something to tell me.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: (Interpretation) I think Mr. Greaves has an observation to make.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) I beg your pardon, Mr. Greaves.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I wanted to catch Your Honours before you disappeared this evening. There was one matter I omitted to deal with at the end of Witness A's evidence. The two statements, one in English and a translation thereof in Bosnian, should properly be admitted as exhibits, not for the truth thereof, but as a matter of impeachment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) No objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: No, no objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Very well. The exhibits have been admitted. What number are they?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: (Interpretation) D1 and D1A for the English version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) The hearing is adjourned. We will resume tomorrow at 2.00 p.m.
